notes.definition: Humans reduce the amount of land available for other animals and plants by building, quarrying, farming and dumping waste. Destroying peat bogs to produce garden compost reduces biodiversity and releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
explanation: As the human population grows and the standard of living rises, more land is used for human activities. Humans reduce the amount of land available for other animals and plants by building (houses, roads, factories and airports), quarrying (digging out rocks, sand, gravel and minerals), farming (fields of crops and grazing land for animals) and dumping waste (landfill sites). Each of these replaces natural habitats with land that very few wild species can use, so populations of many species fall and biodiversity is reduced.

Peat bogs are a special type of habitat. They form in wet areas where the soil is waterlogged and acidic, so there is very little oxygen. Under these conditions the microorganisms that cause decay cannot work well, so dead plant material, mostly Sphagnum moss, only partly decays and builds up as a thick layer of peat. Peat forms very slowly, so a peat bog may have taken thousands of years to develop. Because of this, peat is effectively a non-renewable resource. Peat bogs are home to a distinctive community of plants, animals and microorganisms, including Sphagnum mosses, cotton grass, sundews, insects and wading birds.

Peat has been dug up in large amounts to sell as garden compost, because it holds water well and is useful for growing plants. The destruction of peat bogs, and other areas of peat, to produce garden compost reduces the area of this habitat. This reduces the variety of different plant, animal and microorganism species that live there, which means biodiversity falls. Many of these species are specialised for bog conditions and cannot live anywhere else.

Peat contains a large amount of carbon, stored in the partly decayed plant material. When a bog is drained, air gets into the peat. Microorganisms can then decompose it, and as they respire they release carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. Peat is also burned as a fuel in some places, which releases carbon dioxide directly. Either way, carbon that was locked away for thousands of years is released, increasing the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, which contributes to global warming.

There is a conflict between the demand for cheap peat compost and the need to conserve peat bogs. Gardeners can use peat-free compost instead, made from materials such as composted bark, coconut fibre or garden waste. In the UK the government has announced plans to end the sale of peat compost to amateur gardeners, and some damaged bogs are being restored by blocking drains so they become waterlogged again.
keyFacts: Humans reduce land available for other animals and plants by building, quarrying, farming and dumping waste.
Loss of land and habitats reduces biodiversity.
Peat bogs form in waterlogged, acidic conditions where there is little oxygen, so decay is very slow.
Peat forms very slowly, so it is effectively a non-renewable resource.
Peat bogs are destroyed to produce garden compost.
Destroying peat bogs reduces the area of this habitat and the variety of plant, animal and microorganism species living there.
The decay or burning of peat releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
Peat-free compost is an alternative that helps conserve peat bogs.

keyTerms.definition: The ways humans use land, such as for building, quarrying, farming and dumping waste.
Digging rock, sand, gravel or minerals out of the ground, which removes the habitat on that land.
A soil-like material made of partly decayed plant matter that builds up slowly in waterlogged, acidic bogs. It contains a lot of stored carbon.
A wetland habitat where peat forms because waterlogged, acidic, low-oxygen conditions slow down decay.
The place where an organism lives.
Compost made from materials such as bark, coconut fibre or garden waste instead of peat.
A resource that is used up much faster than it can be replaced.

equations.name: Percentage change
equations.formula: percentage change = (new value − original value) ÷ original value × 100

workedExamples.title: How long does peat take to form?
workedExamples.question: Peat builds up at about 1 mm per year. A machine removes a layer of peat 1.5 m deep. Estimate how long that layer took to form.
steps: Convert to the same units: 1.5 m = 1500 mm.

workedExamples.title: Percentage loss of bog habitat
workedExamples.question: A region had 3200 hectares of peat bog in 1950. By 2010, 2400 hectares had been drained or dug for compost. Calculate the percentage of the original bog that remained in 2010.

workedExamples.title: Explaining carbon release
workedExamples.question: Explain why draining a peat bog increases the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
steps: Draining lets air (oxygen) into the peat.
Microorganisms can now decompose the peat.
The microorganisms respire, releasing carbon dioxide that had been stored in the peat.
workedExamples.answer: Oxygen enters, decomposers break down the peat and release carbon dioxide by respiration.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think peat is renewable because it is made from plants.
misconceptions.right: In fact, peat forms so slowly (about 1 mm per year) that it is used up far faster than it forms, so it is effectively non-renewable.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think peat only releases carbon dioxide if it is burned.
misconceptions.right: In fact, the decay of peat by microorganisms after a bog is drained also releases carbon dioxide.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think farming does not reduce biodiversity because farmland is green.
misconceptions.right: In fact, fields of a single crop or grazing land support far fewer species than the natural habitats they replace.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think destroying a bog only harms plants.
misconceptions.right: In fact, it reduces the variety of plant, animal and microorganism species that live there.

realWorld: Many garden centres in the UK now sell peat-free compost to protect peat bogs.
Conservation groups restore drained bogs by blocking ditches so the peat becomes waterlogged again and Sphagnum moss can regrow.
New housing developments may be required to provide green spaces and wildlife corridors to reduce habitat loss.
Old quarries and landfill sites are sometimes restored as lakes, wetlands or nature reserves after they close.
examTips: Learn the four land uses listed by AQA: building, quarrying, farming and dumping waste.
For peat bogs, make two separate points: loss of habitat reduces biodiversity, and decay or burning releases carbon dioxide.
When explaining carbon dioxide release, say that the decay is carried out by microorganisms that respire.
When asked to evaluate peat use, give both sides: peat is a good growing medium, but its use destroys habitats and releases carbon dioxide.
Use the word biodiversity explicitly and say it is the variety of plant, animal and microorganism species.
summary: Building, quarrying, farming and dumping waste reduce land for other species.
Peat bogs form slowly in waterlogged, acidic, low-oxygen conditions.
Peat bogs are destroyed to make garden compost, reducing biodiversity.
Decay or burning of peat releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
Peat-free compost and bog restoration help to reduce the damage.

questions.question: Which of these human activities reduces the land available for other animals and plants?
options: Planting hedgerows
Quarrying
Creating a nature reserve
Restoring a peat bog
markScheme: 1 mark: quarrying
questions.explanation: Quarrying removes habitats to extract rock and minerals. The other options increase or protect habitats.

questions.question: Why are peat bogs often destroyed?
options: To produce garden compost
To make plastics
To build ships
To produce oxygen
markScheme: 1 mark: to produce garden compost
questions.explanation: Peat is dug up and sold as garden compost because it holds water well.

questions.question: Which gas is released into the atmosphere when peat decays or is burned?
options: Oxygen
Nitrogen
Carbon dioxide
Hydrogen
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Peat contains carbon from plants. Decay (by respiring microorganisms) and burning both release it as carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Which list contains only land uses that AQA states reduce the land available for other animals and plants?
options: Building, quarrying, farming, dumping waste
Building, recycling, farming, planting trees
Quarrying, breeding programmes, farming, fishing
Dumping waste, rewilding, building, recycling
markScheme: 1 mark: building, quarrying, farming, dumping waste
questions.explanation: These four activities are listed in the specification. Recycling, planting trees, breeding programmes and rewilding help biodiversity.

questions.question: Why does dead plant material build up as peat in a bog instead of decaying fully?
options: The bog is too sunny for decomposers
Peat plants are poisonous to animals
There are no microorganisms on Earth that can decay plants
The waterlogged, acidic conditions have little oxygen, so decay is very slow
markScheme: 1 mark: waterlogged, acidic, little oxygen so decay is slow
questions.explanation: Decomposers need oxygen and prefer near-neutral conditions. In bogs, lack of oxygen and acidity slow decay so plant material accumulates.

questions.question: Destroying a peat bog reduces biodiversity. Which statement best explains why?
options: It increases the number of habitats available
It reduces the area of a habitat, so fewer species of plants, animals and microorganisms can live there
It releases oxygen which kills animals
It makes the soil more fertile for crops
markScheme: 1 mark: it reduces habitat area, so fewer species can live there
questions.explanation: The specification states that destroying peat bogs reduces the area of this habitat and thus the variety of species living there.

questions.question: Which is the best alternative for a gardener who wants to protect peat bogs?
options: Use peat-free compost made from bark or garden waste
Use more peat compost
Burn the peat instead of using it
Buy peat from a different country
markScheme: 1 mark: use peat-free compost
questions.explanation: Peat-free compost avoids the destruction of bogs. Buying peat from elsewhere still destroys bogs, and burning peat releases carbon dioxide.

questions.question: A drained peat bog is restored by blocking its ditches. Which is the most likely effect on carbon dioxide release from the peat?
options: It increases, because more plants grow
It stays the same, because peat cannot decay
It decreases, because waterlogging reduces oxygen so decomposers break down less peat
It increases, because the water reacts with peat
markScheme: 1 mark: decreases, because waterlogging reduces oxygen so less decay
questions.explanation: Rewetting the bog removes oxygen from the peat, so microorganisms decompose it much more slowly and less carbon dioxide is released.

questions.question: Peat forms at about 1 mm per year. Which statement best explains why peat is described as a non-renewable resource?
options: Peat cannot form anywhere on Earth today
Peat is made of rock, not plants
Peat forms only in tropical rainforests
Peat is used up much faster than it can form
markScheme: 1 mark: it is used much faster than it forms
questions.explanation: Peat still forms today, but a layer dug in a day may have taken hundreds or thousands of years to accumulate.

questions.question: Peat builds up at a rate of about 1 mm per year. How many years would it take to form a layer of peat 300 mm deep?
markScheme: 1 mark: 300 ÷ 1 = 300 years
questions.explanation: Time = depth ÷ rate = 300 mm ÷ 1 mm per year = 300 years.

questions.question: A peat bog originally covered 4500 hectares. After digging for compost, 1800 hectares remain. Calculate the percentage decrease in the area of the bog.
markScheme: 1 mark: 4500 − 1800 = 2700 hectares
questions.explanation: The area fell by 2700 hectares, and 2700 ÷ 4500 = 0.6, a 60% decrease.

questions.question: Peat forms at 1 mm per year. A peat bog is 4.2 m deep. Estimate the age of the bottom layer of the peat in years.
markScheme: 1 mark: 4.2 m = 4200 mm
1 mark: 4200 ÷ 1 = 4200 years
questions.explanation: Convert metres to millimetres first: 4.2 × 1000 = 4200 mm. At 1 mm per year this took about 4200 years.

questions.question: In a survey, 26 species of plant were found in an area of peat bog. After the bog was drained for peat extraction, only 9 species were found. Calculate the percentage decrease in the number of plant species. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
questions.explanation: 17 ÷ 26 = 0.654, which is 65% to the nearest whole number.

questions.question: A garden centre sold 12 000 bags of compost in a year. 45% of the bags were peat-free. Each peat compost bag contains 0.05 m³ of peat. Calculate the total volume of peat sold in the year.
markScheme: 1 mark: peat bags = 55% of 12 000 = 6600
questions.explanation: If 45% are peat-free then 55% contain peat: 0.55 × 12 000 = 6600 bags. 6600 × 0.05 = 330 m³ of peat.

questions.question: Name two ways in which humans reduce the amount of land available for other animals and plants.
markScheme: 1 mark each, up to 2: building; quarrying; farming; dumping waste
questions.explanation: These four land uses are named in the AQA specification.

questions.question: State what peat is mainly used for when it is dug from bogs.
markScheme: 1 mark: garden compost (accept fuel)
questions.explanation: Most peat dug in the UK has been used as garden compost; in some places it is burned as fuel.

questions.question: Give two reasons why destroying peat bogs is harmful to the environment.
markScheme: 1 mark: reduces the area of habitat, so biodiversity (variety of plant, animal and microorganism species) falls
1 mark: decay or burning of peat releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere
questions.explanation: The two key consequences in the specification are loss of biodiversity and release of carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Explain why draining a peat bog causes the peat to start decaying.
markScheme: 1 mark: draining removes water so air (oxygen) gets into the peat
1 mark: microorganisms (decomposers) can now respire aerobically and break down the peat
questions.explanation: In waterlogged peat there is too little oxygen for most decomposers. Draining removes this limit.

questions.question: Explain how quarrying can reduce biodiversity.
markScheme: 1 mark: quarrying removes the soil, plants and habitat from an area (reduces land available)
1 mark: so fewer species can live there / organisms die or leave, so biodiversity falls
questions.explanation: Quarrying replaces habitat with bare rock and pits, removing the food and shelter species need.

questions.question: A gardener says: 'Peat compost is natural, so using it does no harm to the environment.' Evaluate this statement.
markScheme: 1 mark: peat is natural and a good growing medium (it holds water well)
1 mark: but extracting it destroys bog habitats and reduces biodiversity, and decay or burning releases carbon dioxide
1 mark: conclusion: the statement is wrong because peat forms very slowly (non-renewable); peat-free compost is better
questions.explanation: Being natural does not mean being harmless. The key points are habitat loss, carbon dioxide release and the very slow rate of peat formation.

questions.question: Suggest why the carbon dioxide released from a drained peat bog contributes more to increasing atmospheric carbon dioxide than the carbon dioxide released by a woodland's leaf litter decaying each autumn.
acceptedAnswers: carbon stored for thousands of years
markScheme: 1 mark: the carbon in leaf litter was taken in by photosynthesis recently and is taken in again by the growing trees (balanced cycle)
1 mark: the carbon in peat has been locked away for thousands of years and is not replaced, so it adds to the total in the atmosphere
questions.explanation: Releasing long-stored carbon adds extra carbon dioxide to the atmosphere, whereas leaf litter decay is part of a balanced yearly cycle.

questions.question: Describe how human use of land can reduce biodiversity.
markScheme: Indicative content: building houses, roads and factories replaces habitats; quarrying removes soil, plants and habitats; farming replaces natural habitats with crops (often monocultures) or grazing; dumping waste in landfill uses land and may leak toxic chemicals; destruction of peat bogs for compost removes a specialised habitat; less land available for other animals and plants, fewer species, biodiversity falls.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes at least three land uses and links them clearly to loss of habitat and reduced biodiversity.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): names one or two land uses with little link to biodiversity.
questions.explanation: Answers should name specific land uses and explain that they reduce the land available for other species.

questions.question:
The government of a country plans to ban the sale of peat compost to gardeners. Peat bog companies say this will cost jobs and that gardeners prefer peat because plants grow well in it.
Evaluate the plan to ban the sale of peat compost.
markScheme: Indicative content for the ban: peat bogs are destroyed to produce garden compost; reduces the area of bog habitat; reduces the variety of plant, animal and microorganism species (biodiversity); many bog species are specialised and live nowhere else; draining and digging allows peat to decay, and decay or burning releases carbon dioxide; contributes to global warming; peat forms very slowly (about 1 mm per year) so it is effectively non-renewable; restored bogs can store carbon again.

Against the ban: loss of jobs and income for peat companies and local communities; peat is a good growing medium that holds water; peat-free alternatives may be more expensive or less effective for some plants; peat may simply be imported from other countries, moving the damage elsewhere.

Conclusion: a justified judgement, for example the ban is worthwhile because the environmental damage is long-lasting and peat-free alternatives exist, especially if workers are supported to move into other jobs such as bog restoration.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): balanced evaluation with detailed biological reasons (biodiversity and carbon dioxide) and economic or social points, ending in a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some points for and against with some biological explanation; conclusion may be weak.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple one-sided statements.
questions.explanation: Evaluate questions need both sides and a conclusion. The biological case rests on biodiversity loss and carbon dioxide release; the economic case rests on jobs and gardener preference.

questions.question: A field is used to grow a single crop of wheat instead of being left as wild grassland. What happens to the biodiversity of the field?
options: It increases, because wheat grows quickly
It stays the same, because the field is still green
It decreases, because fewer species can live there
It increases, because the field is fertilised
markScheme: 1 mark: it decreases, because fewer species can live there
questions.explanation: Farming replaces a varied natural habitat with one crop, so many wild species lose their food and shelter.

questions.question: Name the type of organism that releases carbon dioxide when peat decays.
markScheme: 1 mark: microorganisms / decomposers (bacteria or fungi)
questions.explanation: Decay is carried out by microorganisms, which respire and release carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Which of these organisms is most closely linked with the formation of peat?
options: Oak trees
Sphagnum moss
Earthworms
Seaweed
markScheme: 1 mark: Sphagnum moss
questions.explanation: Peat is made mainly of partly decayed Sphagnum moss and other bog plants. Earthworms are decomposers that are rare in acidic, waterlogged bogs, and oak trees and seaweed do not form peat.

questions.question: Suggest two reasons why planners might choose to build a new housing estate on farmland rather than on an area of peat bog.
markScheme: 1 mark each, up to 2: building on the bog would destroy a rare habitat and reduce biodiversity; draining the bog would release carbon dioxide; waterlogged peat is unstable ground to build on; bogs may be protected by law
questions.explanation: Peat bogs support specialised species and store carbon, so destroying them has bigger environmental costs than building on farmland, which already has lower biodiversity.
